items.answer: Non-renewable resource

items.stem: Explain why global energy demand has increased.
items.answer: Population growth; economic development and industrialisation in emerging economies (China, India); rising living standards with more appliances, air conditioning and cars; urbanisation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed reason up to [3]

items.stem: Explain the factors that affect a country’s energy security.
items.answer: Availability of domestic resources; reliance on imports and number of suppliers; political stability of suppliers; infrastructure and storage; diversity of the energy mix; price volatility.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor up to [3]

items.stem: For Germany’s Energiewende or another example of an energy strategy, briefly describe the energy strategy.
items.answer: Germany’s Energiewende: A transition to renewable energy: feed-in tariffs from 2000 encouraged solar and wind; renewables supplied over 50% of electricity by 2023; nuclear power phased out in 2023; coal to be phased out by 2038.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. named sources, data on the energy mix, reasons [4]

items.stem: For geothermal and HEP in Iceland or another example of an energy strategy, briefly evaluate the success of the strategy in providing secure and sustainable energy.
items.answer: geothermal and HEP in Iceland: Very high energy security and low emissions from electricity; but HEP schemes such as Kárahnjúkar flooded wilderness; transport still uses imported oil.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. security, cost, environmental impacts, social impacts; judgement [4]

items.answer: (a) 55.4% (b) Reduce CO₂ emissions to meet targets; reduce dependence on imported fuels (energy security); reduce air pollution; falling costs.

items.stem: Explain the environmental advantages and disadvantages of hydroelectric power.
items.answer: Advantages: no CO₂ emissions during generation, reliable and controllable, reservoir stores water. Disadvantages: flooding of land and habitats, displacement of people, methane from rotting vegetation, blocks fish migration and traps sediment.
items.markingKey: advantage [1]; disadvantages [2] [3]

items.answer: Reduce CO₂ emissions to meet targets; reduce dependence on imported fuels (energy security); reduce air pollution; falling costs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: “Renewable energy can meet all of the world’s energy needs.” Discuss. In your answer you should consider: named countries; intermittency; costs.
items.answer: For: Solar and wind costs have fallen by about 90% and 70% since 2010; countries such as Iceland, Norway, Costa Rica and Paraguay generate nearly all electricity from renewables. Against: Intermittency requires storage and grids; transport, heavy industry and aviation are hard to electrify; materials such as lithium and rare earths are limited; renewables supplied only about 15% of primary energy in the early 2020s. Judgement: Renewables could meet most needs in the long term with storage, efficiency and new technology, but the transition will take decades.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 4 (10-12 marks): detailed, balanced evaluation supported by named examples and a clear, justified conclusion. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, unsupported statements. [12]

items.markingKey: Water stress: when renewable water supply is below about 1700 m³ per person per year. [1]

items.stem: Explain why demand for water is increasing.
items.answer: Population growth; more irrigated agriculture to feed people; industrialisation and energy production; rising living standards (showers, washing machines, diets with more meat); urbanisation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per reason up to [3]

items.stem: Explain the difference between physical and economic water scarcity.
items.answer: Physical scarcity is a natural shortage where demand exceeds supply, e.g. the Middle East; economic scarcity is where water exists but there is no money or infrastructure to supply it, e.g. much of sub-Saharan Africa.
items.markingKey: physical with example [1]; economic with example [1] [2]

items.stem: Refer to your case study of water management in a water-scarce country (for example Israel). Briefly describe the strategies used to increase water supply and manage demand.
items.answer: Israel: Desalination plants (e.g. Sorek) supply about 80% of domestic water; about 85-90% of wastewater is treated and reused for irrigation; drip irrigation was invented and is widely used; national water carrier; strict pricing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. named schemes with data [4]

items.stem: Refer to your case study of water management in a water-scarce country (for example Singapore). Briefly describe the strategies used to increase water supply and manage demand.
items.answer: Singapore: The “four national taps”: local catchment in reservoirs (about two-thirds of land is catchment), imported water from Johor (Malaysia), NEWater (recycled wastewater, about 40% of demand) and desalination (about 25%); plus water pricing, efficiency labels and education.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. named schemes with data [4]

items.stem: With reference to Singapore, or another example of water management in a water-scarce country, evaluate the sustainability of the water management strategies.
items.answer: Model answer (Singapore): Supply has become diverse and secure, with plans to be self-sufficient by 2061 when the Malaysian agreement ends; but desalination and NEWater are energy-intensive and costly.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: economic, social and environmental sustainability; judgement Level 3 (5-6 marks): well-developed points on both sides with examples and a supported conclusion. items.stem: A student writes: “Water scarcity only affects countries with dry climates.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Economic water scarcity affects many wet countries without infrastructure, and over-use can cause scarcity anywhere.

items.stem: Explain the environmental impacts of intensive arable farming.
items.answer: Fertiliser runoff causes eutrophication; pesticides harm non-target species and accumulate in food chains; removal of hedgerows reduces habitats and increases wind erosion; heavy machinery compacts soil; monoculture lowers biodiversity; high fossil fuel use.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed impact up to [4]

items.stem: Explain why meat production has a greater environmental impact than crop production.
items.answer: Energy is lost between trophic levels, so far more land, water and feed are needed per kilogram of food; cattle emit methane; forests are cleared for pasture and feed crops such as soya.
items.markingKey: trophic efficiency [1]; land / water use [1]; methane or deforestation [1] [3]

items.answer: Export earnings, jobs, rural development and tax revenue; food or fuel production for growing demand.

(a) Explain how the farm could reduce its impact on nearby rivers. (b) Suggest why governments in some countries support the expansion of such farms.
items.answer: (a) Buffer strips of vegetation; precise fertiliser application; store manure safely; prevent animals from entering rivers. (b) Export earnings, jobs, rural development and tax revenue; food or fuel production for growing demand.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per method up to [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: “Intensive farming is necessary to feed the world’s growing population.” Discuss. In your answer you should consider: environmental costs; alternatives; Green Revolution.
items.answer: For: Intensive methods (high-yielding varieties, fertiliser, irrigation) roughly tripled cereal production since 1960 and use less land per tonne than extensive systems. Against: Intensive farming causes eutrophication, soil degradation, biodiversity loss and high emissions; about a third of food is wasted; sustainable intensification, agroecology and reducing meat consumption may be better. Judgement: High yields are needed, but they must be achieved sustainably, with less waste and fairer distribution.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 3 (6-8 marks): detailed, balanced discussion using named examples and data, with a reasoned judgement. items.stem: Describe the characteristics of a nomadic pastoral farming system.
items.answer: Herders move with animals (camels, goats, cattle) seasonally to find water and grazing; low inputs; subsistence with some trade; adapted to dry environments such as the Sahel.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per characteristic up to [3]

items.stem: Explain the causes of food insecurity in low-income countries.
items.answer: Poverty prevents people buying food; drought, floods and pests reduce harvests; conflict disrupts farming and supply; poor storage and transport cause losses; rapid population growth; rising food prices.

items.stem: Explain how the Green Revolution increased food production but also caused problems.
items.answer: High-yielding varieties with fertiliser and irrigation doubled or tripled yields; but costs excluded poorer farmers, increased debt and inequality, caused salinisation and falling water tables, pollution from chemicals and loss of crop diversity.

items.answer: It provides a reliable, drought-proof supply for coastal areas (Israel, Saudi Arabia, Singapore); but it is energy-intensive and expensive, emits CO₂ unless renewable energy is used, and returns concentrated brine that harms marine life.

Suggest two strategies that a country with absolute scarcity could use.
items.answer: Desalination; recycling wastewater; importing virtual water as food; drip irrigation and reducing agricultural use; reducing leaks.

items.stem: Ana argues that managing demand is more sustainable than increasing supply for solving water scarcity. Discuss this view, referring to named examples. In your answer you should consider: technology; named countries.
items.answer: For: Drip irrigation, fixing leaks, pricing and grey-water recycling reduce demand cheaply and have few environmental impacts. Against: Rapidly growing cities and dry countries need new supplies: desalination (Israel), recycling (Singapore NEWater) and reservoirs; demand reduction alone may not be enough. Judgement: Demand management should come first as the cheapest and most sustainable option, but most countries need a combination of both.

items.stem: Explain how aquaculture can be both a solution and a problem for fish supply.

items.stem: A coastal city has 500 000 people who each use on average 200 litres of water per day. 25% of the water put into the supply network is lost through leaks. (a) Calculate the volume that must be put into the network each day to allow for leakage. (b) A water-saving campaign reduces use per person by 20%. Calculate the new daily use in m³.
Evaluate the view that managing demand is more sustainable than increasing supply for solving water scarcity. In your answer you should consider: named countries; agriculture; technology.
items.answer: For: Drip irrigation, fixing leaks, pricing and grey-water recycling reduce demand cheaply and have few environmental impacts. Against: Rapidly growing cities and dry countries need new supplies: desalination (Israel), recycling (Singapore NEWater) and reservoirs; demand reduction alone may not be enough. Judgement: Demand management should come first as the cheapest and most sustainable option, but most countries need a combination of both.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 3 (6-8 marks): detailed, balanced discussion using named examples and data, with a reasoned judgement. Level 2 (3-5 marks): developed points but limited balance or exemplification. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generalised points. [8]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “commercial farming”?
options: Farming with low inputs per unit area over large areas, such as cattle ranching.
Farming with high inputs of labour, capital or chemicals per unit area to obtain high yields.
Farming to produce crops or animals for sale at a profit.
Growing a single crop over a large area, often year after year.
items.answer: Farming to produce crops or animals for sale at a profit.
items.markingKey: Commercial farming: farming to produce crops or animals for sale at a profit. [1]

items.stem: Outline one similarity and two differences between commercial farming and subsistence farming.
items.answer: Differences: Subsistence farming produces food mainly for the family with low inputs; commercial farming produces for sale at a profit, often using machinery and chemicals. Similarity: Both depend on climate and soil and can cause land degradation if mismanaged.
items.markingKey: 1 mark similarity; 1 mark per comparative difference up to 2 [3]

items.stem: Approximate water footprints and greenhouse gas emissions per kg of food: chicken 4 300 litres and 7.5 kg CO₂e; milk 1 020 litres and 1.4 kg CO₂e. (a) Calculate the water saved by replacing 1 kg of chicken with the same mass of milk. (b) Suggest one limitation of using water footprint figures to compare foods.
items.answer: (a) 3 280 litres (b) They are global averages; much of the water may be rainfall (green water) rather than irrigation; local scarcity differs.

items.stem: Fig. 6.3 is a systems diagram of a commercial dairy farm in Santiago: inputs include feed, fertiliser, water and energy; processes include milking and grazing; outputs include milk, calves, manure and methane. (a) Describe two environmental impacts of this farming system. (b) Explain how the farm could reduce its impact on nearby rivers.
items.answer: (a) Loss of habitat and biodiversity; greenhouse gas emissions; water pollution from fertilisers and manure; soil degradation. (b) Buffer strips of vegetation; precise fertiliser application; store manure safely; prevent animals from entering rivers.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each up to [2] (b) 1 mark per method up to [2]

items.stem: A news article states: “Sustainable agriculture always produces lower yields.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Methods such as agroforestry, conservation agriculture and integrated pest management can maintain or increase yields over time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the causes of food insecurity in low-income countries. (b) Explain how agroforestry can improve food security and the environment.
items.answer: (a) Poverty prevents people buying food; drought, floods and pests reduce harvests; conflict disrupts farming and supply; poor storage and transport cause losses; rapid population growth; rising food prices. (b) Trees protect soil from erosion, add organic matter and nitrogen (legume trees), provide shade, fuel, fruit and fodder; diverse products reduce risk; trees store carbon and provide habitat.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per cause up to [4] (b) 1 mark per point up to [3]

items.stem: Country P has a population of 5 million and produces 1.5 million tonnes of grain a year. 30% is lost after harvest. Grain provides about 3500 kcal per kg and each person needs about 2100 kcal per day. Suggest two ways of reducing post-harvest losses.
items.answer: Improved storage (hermetic bags, silos) to keep out pests and moisture; better drying; better roads and transport to markets; cold chains.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A Sahel country has a population of 60 million and produces 18.9 million tonnes of grain a year. 15% is lost after harvest. Grain provides about 3500 kcal per kg and each person needs about 2100 kcal per day. (a) Suggest two ways of reducing post-harvest losses. (b) Explain why sufficient food production does not guarantee food security.
items.answer: (a) Improved storage (hermetic bags, silos) to keep out pests and moisture; better drying; better roads and transport to markets; cold chains. (b) People may not be able to afford food (access); distribution may be unequal; food may be exported; diets may lack nutrients (utilisation); supply may be unstable.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark per point up to [2]

items.stem: A Sahel country has a population of 5 million and produces 1.2 million tonnes of grain a year. 20% is lost after harvest. Grain provides about 3500 kcal per kg and each person needs about 2100 kcal per day. (a) Calculate the grain energy available per person per day. (b) Suggest two ways of reducing post-harvest losses.
items.answer: (a) 1 841 kcal (b) Improved storage (hermetic bags, silos) to keep out pests and moisture; better drying; better roads and transport to markets; cold chains.

items.stem: “Technology is the key to achieving global food security.” Discuss. In your answer you should consider: Green Revolution; access and distribution.
items.answer: For: High-yielding and GM varieties, precision farming and irrigation have greatly increased production (Green Revolution); new drought-resistant crops can help adapt to climate change. Against: Food insecurity is mainly caused by poverty, conflict and waste; technology can be costly and damage the environment; land rights, fair trade, reducing waste and empowering women farmers are also essential. Judgement: Technology is necessary but not sufficient; access, distribution and sustainability are as important as production.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 4 (16-20 marks): comprehensive, well-structured essay; detailed knowledge of named examples; sustained evaluation and a well-supported conclusion. Level 3 (11-15 marks): good knowledge and examples, some evaluation, conclusion partly supported. Level 2 (6-10 marks): relevant but mainly descriptive, limited examples or one-sided. Level 1 (1-5 marks): a few simple, generalised points with little or no evaluation. [20]
